summary: Revises the IANA guidelines for allocating new values of the IPv4 Protocol field by removing the Expert Review option from RFC 2780. The change also affects allocation of IPv6 Next Header values. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Each kind of packet has a number tag. This paper changes the rules for who can get a new tag number.

questions: iana allocation for ipv4 protocol field
how do i get a new protocol number

subtitle: Stricter rules for who can get a new Protocol field number

tldr.problem: RFC 2780 allowed three ways to get a new IPv4 Protocol field number: Standards Action, IESG Approval, or Expert Review. The Expert Review path was meant for proprietary protocols under non-disclosure agreements, but this is no longer appropriate given the field's scarcity.
tldr.mechanism: This Best Current Practice removes the Expert Review option, leaving only Standards Action and IESG Approval. This ensures all new protocols have public specifications that can be reviewed before numbering.
tldr.outcome: The Protocol field is limited to 256 possible values with about 55% in use, making conservation important. Removing the secret-protocol path focuses allocations on protocols with public specifications and genuine community need.

today: RFC 5237 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2780. The allocation rules here remain in effect, ensuring that IPv4 Protocol and IPv6 Next Header numbering is reserved for protocols with public specifications.

sections.title: A Scarce Numbering Space
sections.content:
The IPv4 header's Protocol field is an 8-bit number that tells routers what kind of data is inside a packet: TCP is 6, UDP is 17, ICMP is 1. Because it is only 8 bits, there are just 256 possible values. At the time of writing, about 140 were already assigned, leaving room for only about 116 more protocols across all of history.

RFC 2780 set the policy for handing out these scarce numbers. It allowed allocations through three processes: Standards Action (for standards-track RFCs), IESG Approval (for non-standards cases), or Expert Review (for cases with non-disclosure agreements). The Expert Review path was conceived to let vendors develop proprietary protocols privately.
sections.plainLanguage: Only 256 numbers exist, and most are taken. This paper asks: should we still let companies keep their new protocols secret?

sections.title: Why Non-Disclosure No Longer Makes Sense
sections.content:
When RFC 2780 was written in 2000, secret protocols seemed reasonable. By 2008, the Internet had changed. Proprietary protocols for niche use cases no longer justified using precious protocol numbers. Meanwhile, genuinely useful protocols—both standards-track and experimental—needed certainty about their numbering.

The document argues that the field is constrained enough that allocations must balance public interest against vendor interests. A protocol number should go to something with a stable specification and real constituency that will use it, not to a company that wants to reserve a number "just in case."
sections.plainLanguage: We realized that companies mostly don't use secret protocol numbers anyway. We should save them for stuff people actually need.

sections.title: The New Allocation Rules
sections.content:
The new rule is simple: allocate IPv4 Protocol field values through Standards Action or IESG Approval only. Applicants must have a public specification. The IESG Approval path still allows flexibility (for experimental allocations and non-standards uses), but requires a specification that reviewers can read.

The same rule now applies to IPv6 Next Header values, since the IPv6 guidelines reference the IPv4 rules. This harmonizes numbering policy across versions of IP.
sections.plainLanguage: From now on, if you want a protocol number, you have to tell everyone what you're doing. No more secrets.
